name: Robert Youshock
title: Creative Technologist
subtitle: Technical design · Design systems · AI workflows
intro: I turn production problems into shipped technical solutions: automation systems, a Gen-AI virtual-set pipeline, and a 15-station beta pilot run with a vendor's product team. My roots are in broadcast motion design and maps, so everything I build has to look good and hold up on deadline.
available: I'm open to roles in technical design and design systems, AI and code-driven workflow optimization, and pilot or beta program leadership, anywhere the same build-test-scale approach can work beyond broadcast.
education: B.A. Media Production, minor in Creative Technology & Design · CU Boulder
certs: Adobe Certified Professional (After Effects) · Google UX Design · UI/UX Design (Cal Poly) · UX Research & Design (Michigan)
numbers: design, automation and evaluation projects shipped in 2.5 years

tech.title: AXIS Maps beta pilot
tech.body: Led TEGNA's season-long beta of Chyron's AXIS Maps: recruited and managed 20+ field participants across 15 stations, worked directly with Chyron's product and engineering team on feature requests, and built the feature-tracker dashboard used to judge the org-wide rollout.

tech.title: Gen-AI virtual-set pipeline
tech.body: Launched TEGNA's pipeline for AI-rendered virtual sets. I direct the renders in Firefly and Imagen for station projects such as WUSA and WZDX, then hand production-ready sets to the 3D design team.

tech.title: Three automation systems
tech.body: One script re-skins a whole sports league's monitors and open animations (colors, logos, renders) and publishes them to a shared library. Another generates on-brand banners, tiles and marquees for every streaming platform. The third is an After Effects plugin that automates the team's top three daily tasks.

tech.title: Gen-AI enablement program
tech.body: Built the design department's AI training from scratch: prompting in Artlist AI and Firefly, mentoring three tenured designers, and onboarding six new hires into AI workflows from their first week, ahead of the company-wide rollout.

projects.title: TEGNA Election 2024
projects.blurb: From September 2023 through Election Day, I worked with our Art Director and a Senior Designer to build the look and feel of TEGNA's 2024 Elections Package. I built the Chyron Prime templates, the After Effects templates behind the live-updating electoral map, and toolkits for station staff, and I was the bridge between the Motion Design and CG teams. It's my most end-to-end project to date.
projects.problem: Election coverage needs one visual system that can handle fast-moving data, live map updates and station-level customization without losing clarity or consistency.
projects.solution: We developed the package from concept through Election Day. I built the Chyron Prime templates powering the live electoral map, designed map-driven infographics, and created toolkits so every station had a responsive, cohesive package ready for a high-stakes night.

projects.title: Manchester Road Race Map
projects.blurb: Run the course before the runners do. This animated map of the Thanksgiving Day Manchester Road Race, built in Google Earth Studio and After Effects, brought the event to life on WTIC's broadcast with dynamic movement and cinematic clarity.
projects.problem: Static maps miss the excitement and detail of a live race, and leave viewers without a real sense of the course.
projects.solution: I independently built a fully animated course map that pairs accuracy with engaging motion: a broadcast-ready graphic that anchored WTIC's full-day coverage and kept viewers connected to the race.

projects.title: To The Point: Wind Turbines
projects.blurb: A geospatial explainer on California's offshore wind future. Vector infographics and animated maps unpack the promise and the challenges of floating wind turbines off Humboldt County's coast, making a complex climate story clear.
projects.problem: Offshore wind is a data-heavy story full of policy, environmental and community concerns. Traditional reporting struggles to show the scale of the turbines, the economics of port upgrades, or the environmental impact.
projects.solution: I designed and animated a package that combines geospatial maps with vector infographics, turning legislation, costs and environmental concerns into a visual story ABC10 viewers could follow.

projects.title: Key Bridge Collapse
projects.blurb: A broadcast-ready explainer of Baltimore's Key Bridge collapse. With Google Earth Studio and custom vector infographics, the package traced the collision, showed the scale of the disaster, and put its impact in context for WUSA9's coverage.
projects.problem: The collapse was a fast-moving story involving engineering, shipping logistics, lawsuits and rebuilding plans. Footage and static maps couldn't show the scale, or explain why it happened and what came next.
projects.solution: I designed and animated a visual explainer that combines geospatial mapping with infographic storytelling, turning technical details into clear visuals about the tragedy and what it means for Baltimore and national infrastructure.

projects.title: Earthquake Risk
projects.blurb: For KREM's deep dive into Northwest earthquake risk, I built a suite of graphics, including a Google Earth Studio map and vector explainers, that made tectonic science engaging and easy to follow.
projects.problem: Subduction zones, fault lines and volcanic activity feel abstract and overwhelming to most viewers, and charts or static images rarely capture the scale, urgency or geography.
projects.solution: I created a package that pairs Google Earth Studio mapping with custom vector diagrams of tectonic plates, earthquake terms and seismic hazards, bringing scientific depth to KREM's coverage while keeping it easy to understand.

projects.title: Airbag Recall
projects.blurb: A broadcast breakdown of why more than 457,000 Ford and Mazda vehicles were under urgent "Do Not Drive" orders over faulty Takata airbag inflators, combining geospatial visuals, motion-driven data layers and infographic storytelling.
projects.problem: It's the largest auto safety recall in U.S. history, yet millions of dangerous inflators remain unrepaired. The challenge was communicating that urgency clearly.
projects.solution: I built a visual package that layers animated geospatial overlays with infographics broken down by make, model and urgency, showing the scope, the human toll (27 deaths, 400+ injuries) and the free fix, with a clear call to check your VIN.

sides.title: Our Places
sides.blurb: A phone-first web app for two people to keep a top 10 in every food category, plus a wish list of places to try. It has a map with category pins, offline mode, drag to re-rank, and Spotify Wrapped-style story cards drawn on the phone. It runs for $0 a month.
sides.built: Vanilla JS, Cloudflare Pages + D1, MapLibre
sides.problem: Two people, dozens of favorite spots, and the same question every weekend: where should we eat? Notes apps and map lists don't rank anything, don't sync cleanly between two phones, and don't remember what to order.
sides.solution: I designed and built a home-screen app where every category gets a ranked top 10 and a wish list, synced between both phones and usable with no signal. Design came first: two visually distinct lists, a food-icon map, and a warm type-driven look. The whole stack runs on free tiers with daily caps, so it can never send a bill.

sides.title: Cairn
sides.blurb: A free web tool for finding a US map boundary in plain words, checking it on the map, and downloading it for Google Earth, a GPS watch or mapping software. It's built for people who have never opened ArcGIS, and it's quick enough for people who use it every day.
sides.built: Vanilla JS, MapLibre, Census and ArcGIS data
sides.problem: Public map data is easy to find and hard to trust. A normal search returns ten results with the same name: some are empty, some are tables with no shapes, and some label every shape with an ID number. Getting one clean boundary file usually means knowing GIS software.
sides.solution: Cairn understands plain words like "texas state house", opens and checks every result before showing it, and ranks the nearest first. It exports KML, KMZ, GPX or GeoJSON and shows the file size before you download. There's no account and no server: the browser talks straight to the data publishers, so it costs nothing to run.
